How would you version and roll out a pro: Store prompts in version control alongside application code (not hardcoded strings scattered across the codebase, and not edited live in a provider's UI), tag each prompt version, and run every change through the same evaluation suite used for model changes before deploy. Roll out via canary - route a small percentage of traffic to the new prompt version, compare its eval scores/user feedback against the current version, and promote fully only once it's validated, with the previous version immediately available for rollback exactly like any other code deployment.
How would you track and control LLM API: Tag every request with metadata identifying the team/feature/user making it, log token usage (prompt + completion) per request into a cost-tracking table, and aggregate into a per-team cost dashboard with budget alerts. For control (not just visibility), route requests through an internal gateway/proxy that enforces per-team quotas and rate limits at the API-key or header level, so one team's runaway usage can't silently consume the shared account's budget or rate limit before anyone notices.
What would you monitor for a production: Token usage and cost per request (and trends over time), latency broken down by time-to-first-token versus total generation time (important for streaming UX), output quality signals (a sampled LLM-as-judge score, or user feedback like thumbs up/down), hallucination/faithfulness rate if grounded in RAG, and rate of fallback/error responses or refused requests - uptime alone tells you the service responded, not whether what it responded with was actually good or safe.
How would you build a regression test su: Build a golden dataset of representative inputs paired with expected properties or a scoring rubric rather than exact-match expected outputs, and score using a combination of automated checks (schema validity, keyword presence) and an LLM-as-judge pass against the rubric. Run each test case multiple times (e.g. 3-5 samples) and evaluate the pass rate/score distribution rather than a single pass/fail, since non-determinism means one lucky or unlucky sample isn't a reliable signal - a prompt version passing 5/5 is meaningfully better than one passing 3/5 even though both 'passed' at least once.
What is prompt caching, and how does it: Prompt caching lets a provider (or your own infrastructure) reuse the already-processed representation of a repeated prompt prefix - e.g. a long, unchanging system prompt or document context - so only the new, variable part of the request needs full processing, cutting both cost and latency significantly for requests sharing a large common prefix. It's most valuable for applications with a large static system prompt/context reused across many requests (a RAG system re-sending the same document context, or a chatbot with a long persona/instruction prompt), and is worth explicitly designing prompts to maximize a stable, cacheable prefix where possible.
How would you design rate limiting and q: Issue each team a scoped API key/service account with token-per-minute and request-per-minute quotas enforced at a gateway layer in front of the actual provider, so one team's traffic spike or bug can't starve capacity from others - the same bulkhead pattern used for any shared internal service. Layer this with cost-based budgets (not just rate-based), since a team could stay within rate limits while still running up disproportionate cost via very large prompts/contexts.
How would you handle a production incide: This is why pinning to a specific model version (not a floating alias like 'latest') matters in the first place - if you weren't pinned and got silently auto-upgraded, the immediate fix is pinning to the last known-good version if the provider still supports it, or rolling forward with prompt adjustments validated against your eval suite if not. Long-term, treat model version changes with the same rigor as a dependency upgrade: run the full eval suite against the new version before intentionally adopting it, rather than being passively auto-upgraded and discovering behavior changes reactively in production.
What observability tools (LangSmith, Lan: These tools capture LLM-specific trace detail generic APM doesn't - the exact prompt sent, every intermediate reasoning/tool-call step in an agent chain, token counts and cost per step, and the full input/output at each stage of a RAG or multi-step pipeline. Generic APM shows you a request took 2 seconds and returned 200 OK; an LLM observability tool shows you which of five chained LLM calls consumed 80% of that time, exactly what was retrieved for a RAG query, and lets you replay/debug a specific problematic production request end-to-end - this level of detail is essential for debugging non-deterministic, multi-step LLM pipelines in a way generic request/response logging can't support.
How would you implement human-in-the-loo: Don't block the response on human review for the common path - serve the LLM's output immediately, and asynchronously sample a percentage of interactions (or specifically flag ones matching risk criteria - low confidence, a sensitive topic, a high-stakes action) into a review queue for a human to check after the fact. For genuinely high-risk actions where review must happen before anything proceeds (an agent about to take a destructive action), gate only that specific action type behind synchronous approval, rather than adding review latency to the entire system uniformly.
How would you handle PII/sensitive data: Scrub/redact PII before it ever reaches the model or gets logged (a pre-processing filter detecting and masking emails, names, SSNs, etc.), confirm and configure the provider's data usage policy explicitly (many enterprise API tiers contractually guarantee prompts aren't used for training, but this must be verified and configured, not assumed), and apply the same retention/access controls to LLM interaction logs that you'd apply to any other system handling sensitive data, since prompt/response logs are a real data store that needs the same governance as a database.
What is the role of an LLM gateway/proxy: A gateway centralizes cross-cutting concerns that would otherwise be duplicated in every application calling an LLM - authentication/API key management, rate limiting and quota enforcement per team, cost tracking and logging, model routing/fallback logic, and a consistent interface abstracting away provider-specific API differences. This lets application teams call one internal, consistent endpoint without each reimplementing quota enforcement, cost tracking, and fallback logic independently, and gives the platform team a single place to add new models or change providers without every consuming application needing a code change.
How would you design CI/CD for a GenAI a: Version prompts, RAG index configuration (chunking parameters, embedding model version), and application code together as one coherent deployable unit, run the full evaluation suite (testing the combination, not each piece in isolation) on every change, and promote through environments with the same gates as any other deployment - a canary/staged rollout with automated eval-score comparison against the current production version, and automatic rollback if the new combination regresses. Treating any one of prompts/index/code as independently deployable risks a mismatch (a prompt assuming an index structure that hasn't actually been updated yet) that's hard to debug after the fact.
How would you decide when to deprecate/s: Treat it like any API deprecation - announce a deprecation timeline with enough lead time for consumers to migrate, monitor actual usage of the old version to know who's still depending on it, and use versioned endpoints/prompt identifiers so consumers explicitly opt into a version rather than silently getting auto-upgraded or auto-broken. Only fully remove the old version once usage has dropped to zero (or all remaining consumers have been directly contacted and confirmed migrated), rather than assuming a deprecation notice alone guarantees everyone actually moved off it in time.
